growth_story.headline: Mexico's income per person has crept up 0.8 percent a year since 1990, knocked back by three deep crises, and in 2025 stood near its 2016 level.
growth_story.arc: Mexico's income per person has grown slowly since 1990, at 0.8 percent a year on average over 1990–2025, with no lasting change of pace in the data. Three deep falls broke that slow climb: 7.6 percent in 1995 in the tequila crisis, 7.7 percent in 2009 when factory output collapsed through its close ties to the United States, and 9.1 percent in 2020 in the pandemic. Income per person came back each time, but gains between shocks were modest, and the sources link this to long-standing low productivity and weak investment. Growth slowed to 0.3 percent a year over 2016–2025, from 0.6 in the decade before; income per person peaked in 2018 and in 2025 was 0.4 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 2016. After a rebound of 5.3 percent in 2021, growth faded to 0.5 percent in 2024 and income per person fell 0.3 percent in 2025, as fiscal tightening, tight monetary policy and trade uncertainty weighed on the economy.

threads.title: Debt and tequila crises, then 2009
threads.text: The 1982 debt crisis and the 1995 tequila crisis left Mexico with high deficits and debt; income per person fell 7.6 percent in 1995. In 2009 income per person fell 7.7 percent as factory output collapsed through Mexico's close ties to the United States, including car production.

threads.title: Pandemic fall, slow recovery
threads.text: Income per person fell 9.1 percent in 2020, the deepest drop in the record since 1990, and rebounded 5.3 percent in 2021. The OECD describes the recovery from the pandemic as slow.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2024

threads.title: Weak productivity and investment
threads.text: The OECD and World Bank both describe low productivity and weak investment as long-running features of the economy. The World Bank points to gaps in infrastructure and energy, insecurity, regulatory uncertainty, limited finance and skills.

threads.title: Nearshoring hopes, US trade doubts
threads.text: In 2024 the OECD saw firms moving supply chains closer to the United States as a new opening for Mexico. Since 2025, trade uncertainty, including doubts over the North American trade agreement, has weighed on investment, alongside tighter fiscal and monetary policy.

since_last_year.text: Income per person fell 0.3 percent in 2025 as the economy slowed. In 2026, rising real incomes from work and earlier interest-rate cuts supported spending at home, while trade uncertainty and fiscal restraint held back investment. In October 2026 the IMF expected growth to stay limited, mainly by uncertainty abroad, including the review of the trade agreement with the United States and Canada.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Mexico (October 2026)
citations.quote: Rising real labor incomes and earlier monetary easing supported domestic demand, but trade uncertainty and fiscal restraint weighed on investment.

citations.title: México: Declaración del personal técnico al término de la misión del Artículo IV correspondiente a 2026
citations.quote: Se proyecta que el crecimiento alcance 1.5% en 2026 y 1.8% en 2027, aunque seguiría limitado, principalmente por la incertidumbre externa.

growth_story.tension: The sources' growth figures are for the whole economy and look modest but steady; income per person grew far more slowly, 0.8 percent a year over 1990–2025, because the population kept growing. And while the OECD described nearshoring as a new opening in 2024, income per person in 2025 was still 0.4 percent below its 2018 peak and about where it first was in 2016.
